According to the paper, HRD should respond in several ways.

- Lovett says HRD should shift its focus from individual capability to the collective system that produces it.
- He proposes measuring the health of the commons with indicators such as entry-level hiring ratios. These indicators are offered as a research agenda, not as validated measurement instruments.
- Governance could form at three levels: organizations, professional associations and public policy. Associations in medicine, law and engineering already have infrastructure that could support experimentation.
- The paper cites Ostrom's eight design principles, which she introduced in her 1990 book Governing the Commons.
- On public policy, he favors investment over prohibition, such as training subsidies and tax credits for firms that keep developmental pipelines. He treats these proposals as hypotheses to test rather than firm recommendations.
- HRD professionals will need systems thinking in addition to skill with AI tools.

Since the losses appear years later, firms are unlikely to change on their own without outside coordination. The paper estimates that the shortage of experienced workers will become visible between 2030 and 2045. It estimates that the shortage will cost the U.S. economy $1 trillion a year by 2040. Mentoring programs are the cheapest and most effective fix, according to the paper.

The paper also draws on Pigou's idea of a negative externality from 1920. Pigou was a Cambridge economist best known for proposing taxes on pollution. Lovett served for twenty years as a military training officer before turning to research.

Participants in your reading group might enjoy debating this.
